newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China launches Opium War film in HK, snubs Patten.
newsitem.headline: China launches Opium War film in HK, snubs Patten.

text.p: China launched its Opium War movie epic in Hong Kong on Wednesday and snubbed last British Governor Chris Patten by excluding him from the guest list.
The blockbuster depicts Britain wresting Hong Kong from the Qing Dynasty's empire in a national humiliation set to end when Britain returns the territory at midnight on June 30.
Patten, the 28th of the British governors that the 19th century opium war ushered into Hong Kong, was not invited.
Times have changed since a stuffy colonial era's society revolved around the governor, but it is still rare for his name not to head the list of invitees at VIP events.
The top guests at the premiere of "The Opium War", screened on Wednesday night, were representatives of the new Hong Kong who take power as he sails away, ending 156 years of British rule.
They include his successsor, future leader Tung Chee-hwa, the president of the incoming legislature Rita Fan and the deputy chief of China's Hong Kong mission, Zhang Junsheng.
"We haven't received an invitation," Patten's spokesman Kerry McGlynn told Reuters. "He has read reports about the movie. But he has not expressed an interest in seeing it."
He added that the governor is a keen movie fan and recently saw "The Gate of Heavenly Peace," a documentary about China's bloody 1989 crackdown against student-led democracy protests.

"If the film on the Opium War is as balanced and as objective, then I'm sure it will have some credibility. If it isn't, if it's seen as something else, Hong Kong people will in their usual wise way make their own judgment," McGlynn said.
Little love is lost between Patten and China, or between Patten and the post-colonial government-in-waiting.
Beijing and its followers in Hong Kong have blamed Patten for complicating the handover by introducing democratic reforms in the twilight years of British rule without Beijing's consent.
More than 1,000 guests were invited by the organiser of the Opium War premiere in Hong Kong, Panasia Films, to twin screenings at the Hong Kong Convention Centre.
Officials at Panasia Films said they were too busy to comment about Patten's absence from the invitation list.
Chinese officials have hailed "The Opium War" as a major event in China's movie history and a contribution to national efforts to mark Hong Kong's return to Beijing's rule.
Britain seized Hong Kong away from the Celestial Empire in 1841 in a war over opium trade which China abhorred.

Made with a budget of US$12 million and a cast of 50,000 including 3,000 non-Chinese, "The Opium War" was launched in the Chinese capital on Tuesday. Director Xie Jin said he hoped it would be seen worldwide, not just by Chinese.

Xie has sought to compare the Opium War, triggered by Beijing's attempts to stop Western shipments of the narcotic, to Nazi Germany's massacre of the Jews and China's ultra-leftist 1966-76 Cultural Revolution. Chinese officials in the 19th century warned that opium threatened to reduce whole provinces to a stupor.
He likens the movie to Stephen Spielberg's acclaimed "Schindler's List," a film about the Holocaust.
The director insists his 140-minute epic is not propaganda.
But the presence at the Beijing premiere of Li Tieying, a member of the elite Politburo, and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, signified clear approval by China's culture commissars.
The historic epic will be shown on general release in Hong Kong cinemas from Friday.
